SEPARATE WRITING DISPOSING OF TANGIBLE PERSONAL PROPERTY (PROB. CODE §§ 6130-6132; SIMON V. GRAYSON; ESTATE OF SMITH) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Katherine A. Seeligsohn · March 25, 2019

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about a separate writing that disposes of a testator's tangible personal property — the kind of list or memorandum that a will refers to but that is not itself signed and witnessed as a will. It describes Probate Code section 6132, which lets a will refer to such a writing and sets the conditions the writing must satisfy; what that section counts as "tangible personal property" and what it excludes; the dollar limits it places on the property such a writing may dispose of; how the writing must be dated, handwritten or signed, and how specific it must be; what happens when the writing is undated or does not meet the handwriting-or-signature condition; what the section provides when a person named in the writing dies before the testator; the personal representative's duty to file the writing during probate; and how section 6132 sits alongside the two older doctrines in the same chapter — incorporation by reference under section 6130 and dispositions by reference to acts and events of independent significance under section 6131 — and alongside the execution formalities that Probate Code sections 6110 and 6111 require of a will itself. It is prepared as background in connection with the will of Katherine A. Seeligsohn dated March 25, 2019, the separate writing dated July 3, 2023, and any administration of that estate by Martin E. Green in Alameda County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not state whether any particular writing satisfies section 6132, whether any item falls inside or outside its limits, or what any person should do.

WHAT PROBATE CODE SECTION 6132 PERMITS AND THE THREE CONDITIONS IT IMPOSES
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (a), provides that notwithstanding any other provision, a will may refer to a writing that directs disposition of tangible personal property not otherwise specifically disposed of by the will, with two categories carved out of what such a writing may reach: money that is common coin or currency, and property used primarily in a trade or business. The same subdivision makes the writing effective only if all three of the conditions it lists are satisfied — an unrevoked will refers to the writing; the writing is dated and is either in the handwriting of, or signed by, the testator; and the writing describes the items and the recipients of the property with reasonable certainty. Section 6132 was added by Statutes 2006, chapter 280, and took effect on January 1, 2007. It sits in Chapter 4 of Part 1 of Division 6 of the Probate Code, titled "Reference to Matters Outside the Will," together with section 6130 (incorporation by reference) and section 6131 (acts and events of independent significance). Whether the writing dated July 3, 2023 satisfies each of those three conditions, and whether any item it names was otherwise specifically disposed of by the will of Katherine A. Seeligsohn dated March 25, 2019, are questions this sheet does not answer.

WHAT SECTION 6132 DEFINES AS "TANGIBLE PERSONAL PROPERTY" AND AS "COMMON COIN OR CURRENCY"
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (h), supplies two definitions that fix the reach of the section. Under subdivision (h)(1), "tangible personal property" means articles of personal or household use or ornament, including but not limited to furniture, furnishings, automobiles, boats, and jewelry, as well as precious metals in any tangible form, such as bullion or coins and articles held for investment purposes; the same paragraph states what the term does not mean — real property, a mobilehome as defined in section 798.3 of the Civil Code, and intangible property such as evidences of indebtedness, bank accounts and other monetary deposits, documents of title, and securities. Under subdivision (h)(2), "common coin or currency" — the money excluded by subdivision (a) — means the coins and currency of the United States that are legal tender for the payment of public and private debts, but does not include coins or currency kept or acquired for their historical, artistic, collectable, or investment value apart from their normal use as legal tender for payment. Whether any particular item named in the writing dated July 3, 2023 falls within either definition is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE DOLLAR LIMITS: $25,000 IN TOTAL AND $5,000 FOR ANY ONE ITEM (PROB. CODE § 6132(G))
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (g), places two dollar limits on a separate writing. First, the total value of tangible personal property identified and disposed of in the writing shall not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars. Second, if the value of an item of tangible personal property described in the writing exceeds five thousand dollars, that item shall not be subject to the section and shall instead be disposed of pursuant to the remainder clause of the will. The subdivision then states how the two limits interact: the value of an item that is disposed of pursuant to the remainder clause of the will shall not be counted towards the twenty-five thousand dollar limit. The statute states these figures as fixed dollar amounts and contains no provision adjusting them for inflation. Whether the property identified in the writing dated July 3, 2023 exceeds either limit, and what any item is worth, are questions this sheet does not answer.

WHEN THE WRITING MAY BE MADE, CHANGES TO IT, AND ITS EFFECT (PROB. CODE § 6132(C), (D))
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (c), addresses timing and effect. It provides that the writing may be written or signed before or after the execution of the will and need not have significance apart from its effect upon the dispositions of property made by the will — a departure from the two older doctrines in the same chapter, under which a writing incorporated by reference must be in existence when the will is executed (section 6130) and a reference to acts and events works only where those acts and events have significance apart from their effect on the will's dispositions (section 6131). The same subdivision provides that a writing meeting the section's requirements shall be given effect as if it were actually contained in the will itself. Subdivision (d) provides that the testator may make subsequent handwritten or signed changes to any writing, and that if there is an inconsistent disposition of tangible personal property as between writings, the most recent writing controls. Whether the writing dated July 3, 2023 was made before or after the will of Katherine A. Seeligsohn dated March 25, 2019, and whether any later writing displaces it, are questions this sheet does not answer.

AN UNDATED WRITING: INCONSISTENCY AND TESTAMENTARY CAPACITY (PROB. CODE § 6132(E))
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (a)(2), requires that the writing be dated. Subdivision (e) states what follows when a date is missing. Under subdivision (e)(1), if the writing omits a statement as to the date of its execution, and if the omission results in doubt whether its provisions or the provisions of another writing inconsistent with it are controlling, then the writing omitting the statement is invalid to the extent of its inconsistency unless the time of its execution is established to be after the date of execution of the other writing. Under subdivision (e)(2), if the writing omits a statement as to the date of its execution and it is established that the testator lacked testamentary capacity at any time during which the writing may have been executed, the writing is invalid unless it is established that it was executed at a time when the testator had testamentary capacity. The structure mirrors the rule Probate Code section 6111, subdivision (b), applies to an undated holographic will. Whether the writing dated July 3, 2023 carries a date sufficient for subdivision (e), and whether Katherine A. Seeligsohn had testamentary capacity at any relevant time, are questions this sheet does not answer.

A WRITING THAT IS NOT HANDWRITTEN OR SIGNED: WHAT SUBDIVISION (B) PRESERVES
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (a)(2), requires that the writing be dated and be either in the handwriting of, or signed by, the testator. Subdivision (b) provides that the failure of a writing to conform to the conditions described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) does not preclude the introduction of evidence of the existence of the testator's intent regarding the disposition of tangible personal property as authorized by the section. Separately, Probate Code section 6111.5 provides that extrinsic evidence is admissible to determine whether a document constitutes a will pursuant to section 6110 or 6111, or to determine the meaning of a will or a portion of a will if the meaning is unclear. Whether any evidence would be admitted or believed in any proceeding concerning the writing dated July 3, 2023, and what subdivision (b) permits such evidence to establish, are questions this sheet does not answer.

IF A PERSON NAMED IN THE WRITING DIES BEFORE THE TESTATOR (PROB. CODE § 6132(C))
Probate Code section 6132, subdivision (c), provides that a writing meeting the section's requirements shall be given effect as if it were actually contained in the will itself, except that if any person designated to receive property in the writing dies before the testator, the property shall pass as further directed in the writing and, in the absence of any further directions, the disposition shall lapse. California's anti-lapse statute, Probate Code section 21110, subdivision (a), provides separately that, subject to subdivision (b), if a transferee is dead when the instrument is executed, or fails or is treated as failing to survive the transferor or until a future time required by the instrument, the issue of the deceased transferee take in the transferee's place in the manner provided in section 240, and subdivision (b) provides that the issue of a deceased transferee do not take in the transferee's place if the instrument expresses a contrary intention or a substitute disposition. How those two provisions operate together, and what would become of any gift in the writing dated July 3, 2023 to a person who did not survive Katherine A. Seeligsohn, are questions this sheet does not answer.

INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE (PROB. CODE § 6130) AND THE REQUIREMENT THAT THE WRITING ALREADY EXIST
Probate Code section 6130 provides that a writing in existence when a will is executed may be incorporated by reference if the language of the will manifests this intent and describes the writing sufficiently to permit its identification. In Simon v. Grayson the California Supreme Court stated the doctrine as settled law in this state: a testator may incorporate an extrinsic document into a will, provided the document is in existence at the time and provided further that the reference to it in the will clearly identifies it or renders it capable of identification by extrinsic proof. The same opinion stated the reason an attempt to incorporate a future document is ineffectual, and stated the standard of identification: the informal document need not be identified with exact precision; it is enough that the descriptive words and extrinsic circumstances combine to produce a reasonable certainty that the document in question is the one referred to by the testator in the will. expectedJSON.body: Probate Code section 6130 provides that a writing in existence when a will is executed may be incorporated by reference if the language of the will manifests this intent and describes the writing sufficiently to permit its identification. In Simon v. Grayson the California Supreme Court stated the doctrine as settled law in this state: a testator may incorporate an extrinsic document into a will, provided the document is in existence at the time and provided further that the reference to it in the will clearly identifies it or renders it capable of identification by extrinsic proof. Simon also applied the principle that a codicil republishes the will it modifies, so that a document in existence when the codicil was executed could be incorporated even though it postdated the will.
